Equity Strategy
A stock pickers' market with diverging performance

China equities posted divergent performance in 2Q: MSCI China/HSCEI fell 7.6%/9.8%, while ChiNext/STAR 50 surged 38.6%/78.6%, highlighting the gap between internet-heavy HK benchmarks and A-share growth indices. Globally, macro events (eg Iran conflict, the Trump-Xi meeting) had limited market impact, while AI capex drove earnings upgrades across tech supply chains. Positioning became more concentrated and crowded, volatility is elevated, and retail leverage (incl leveraged ETFs) amplified market swings. Sentiment became more fragile amid inflation and liquidity concerns. We continue to view China as a stock pickers' market, with A-shares likely to outperform H-shares until the global AI rally unwinds. We maintain our barbell strategy, favoring both value/yield and sectors with strong earnings support and R.E.A.L. moats.
Market: inexpensive, but not yet compelling

MSCI China fell 7.6% in 2Q26 in USD terms, underperforming global markets (vs MSCI World: +14.5%, MSCI EM: +23.3%). Within MSCI China, IT was the only sector with positive return in 2Q (+36.7%), while Consumer Discretionary (-20.7%), Consumer Staples (-18.6%) and Materials (-18.3%) were the worst performers. The index currently trades at 10.3x forward P/E, a 12% discount to its long-term average, but still above the historical trough of 8-9x. Earnings remain challenged, with consensus 2026E EPS growth revised down from 11-12% in Jan to 2-3% now. Flow-wise, liquidity pressures are building in 3Q, with nearly HKD540bn of lock-up expiries and a strong IPO pipeline.
Macro: uneven growth with continued domestic softness

China Investment Compass (CIM) should mostly be in the C4/stimulating phase in 2026. Credit growth slowed from 8.2% in 2025 to 7.7% in 1Q26 and 7.4% in May, alongside weak domestic demand. FAI declined 4.1% YoY, while retail sales rose just 1.4% in 5M26. Exports remained a bright spot (+15.5% YoY in 5M26), but the uneven growth caps investor conviction on China equities. PPI turned positive in Mar-26, after 41 consecutive months of deflation, and rose to 3.9% by May, driving a strong industrial profit growth of 18.8% YoY in 5M26. However, sustainability is questionable given the lower energy prices. Expectations for near-term policy stimulus remain muted.
Model portfolio: industrials/tech over utilities/consumers

For 3Q26, our quant-driven portfolio upgrades industrials (incl. heavy machinery and electrical equipment) and tech hardware to the Top-10 OW list. We stay positive on communications equipment, which was up 92% in 2Q. We also upgrade diversified financials for strong 2Q earnings, and remain constructive on metals & mining (ex-gold), chemicals, and life sciences sectors. On the other hand, our model downgrades IPPs & renewables and liquors to the Bottom-10 UW list, while remains cautious on the autos, gas & water utilities, real estate, biotech, and household durables sectors.

Market performance review

2Q26 was marked by AI-led market leadership, resulting in sharper divergence between tech and non-tech sectors and between A- and H-shares. While investors increasingly looked through geopolitical headlines, concerns over weak domestic demand and an export-reliant economy continued to cap conviction on China equities. In USD terms, KOSPI (+64.2%), ChiNext (+38.6%), and Nikkei 225 (+34.1%) outperformed in 2Q26, while HSCEI (-9.8%), HSI (-7.7%), and MSCI China (-7.6%) lagged. Within MSCI China, IT was the only sector with positive return in 2Q (+36.7%), while Consumer Discretionary (-20.7%), Consumer Staples (-18.6%) and Materials (-18.3%) were the worst performers. A/H-share divergence widened notably: CSI 300 +13.7% in 2Q, while HSCEI -9.8%. P/E valuation of MSCI China fell back to 10.3x, which is a 12% discount to its long-term average, but still above the historical trough of 8-9x.

AI investing became increasingly nuanced in 2Q26, as markets grappled with shifting narratives around memory supercycles, CPO deployment delays, domestic GPU substitution, and internet platforms' AI monetization. However, a series of brief but sharp sentiment resets from late May highlighted growing investor discomfort. Concentrated holdings, elevated volatility, retail leverage (including leveraged ETFs), and rising inflation and liquidity concerns contributed to increasingly jittery market sentiment. Global yield breakouts, a muted Trump-Xi summit, China's cross-border capital flow tightening, and renewed geopolitical uncertainty further triggered periodic de-risking. The narrow rally also widened the divergence between A-shares and H-shares. China's AI localization theme remained a key source of support for onshore equities, while the offshore Hong Kong market, with lower exposure to domestic semiconductor champions and higher weights in internet and financial stocks, was more vulnerable to earnings risks, macro headwinds, and domestic policy actions.

Policy actions in 2Q26 appeared more targeted, in contrast to the broad-based margin requirement tightening in January. In late May, regulators launched a two-year crackdown on illegal cross-border investment by mainland investors and penalized three online brokers. In addition, the State Council issued Order No. 837 on Outbound Investment, expanding oversight to resident individuals and embeds national security, export control, and cross-border compliance considerations into overseas investment activities. Meanwhile, Chinese tax authorities have stepped up scrutiny of overseas income and assets reported through CRS (Common Reporting Standard) information-sharing mechanisms, prompting investor concerns on outbound wealth flows and offshore asset holdings. These developments raised worries over Hong Kong's liquidity and its insurance, wealth management, and property sectors. Separately, regulatory overhang on large internet platforms resurfaced, as evidenced by SAMR-led actions targeting platform marketing practices during the "618" shopping festival, food delivery competition and safety standards, and online train-ticketing services.

Vibrant IPO market is bright spot amid tech boom, with A-share IPO fundraising +89% YoY to USD10bn in 1H26 and HK proceeds +91% YoY to USD27bn, the strongest first-half on record. Concerns of capital rotation away from existing holdings to fund new offerings, as well as selling pressure from upcoming lock-up expirations of recently listed names, increasingly weighed on near-term sentiment.

Macro activity data in Apr-May pointed to further weakness in domestic demand and investment, and economic growth became increasingly reliant on exports. Policy direction remained broadly consistent. The new overnight rate framework signals higher tolerance for lower rates, while fiscal spending YTD appeared more delayed and conditional. Apr Politburo meeting readout indicated no rush on stimulus and highlighted economic resilience, as market expected. The Lujiazui forum in Jun unveiled a narrower short-term rate corridor (50bp vs. 70bp previously) to improve short-term liquidity guidance, introduced a new “FIMA RMB Repo” to supply offshore yuan liquidity, and relaxed STAR listing criteria to accommodate pre-profit AI model companies.

Geopolitics remained an overhang across Asian markets, but its marginal influence diminished during 2Q26, particularly for A-shares. Investors looked through geopolitical shocks and focused on regions and sectors with stronger AI fundamentals, notably Korea and Taiwan, while China relatively underperformed.

On US-China relations, the Trump-Xi summit in May delivered modest economic agreements, although progress on core disputes remained limited. A positive takeaway was Trump's invitation for Xi to visit the White House in Sep-2026, providing a degree of near-term policy stability. China was also not singled out in the Section 301 findings released in early June; the 12.5% tariff was imposed alongside measures targeting multiple major trading partners over forced-labor concerns. That said, geopolitical and reputational risks continue to rise as new restrictions emerge. In June, the Pentagon updated its Section 1260H list of entities with alleged military ties, adding several major Chinese companies, including Alibaba, Baidu, BYD, CXMT, and Unitree.

Valuation and earnings revision

The average 12mth forward P/E valuation for the CSI 300 index rose to 14.9x, 11% above its long-term average, while MSCI China Index traded at 10.3x as of 2Q26, a 12% discount to average. Vast majority of the MSCI China sectors were below their historical average P/E levels. IT and Real Estate were the notable exceptions, trading at 80% and 40% premiums to their historical average, respectively. By contrast, Consumers and Energy had the largest discount, at 32-35% below their long-term average levels.

China flow lens
Domestic capital offsets weak foreign inflows

The recovery in foreign fund inflows highlighted in our China Flow Lens, 12 June 2026 proved short-lived. Following a strong rebound in May, foreign-domiciled China equity funds tracked by EPFR recorded net outflows of USD2.1bn in the four weeks ended 1 July. At the market level, A-share funds saw net redemptions of USD523.1mn, reversing from net inflows of USD347.4mn in the four weeks ended 27 May. Meanwhile, inflows into Hong Kong-focused funds also moderated notably, declining from USD587.5mn to USD347.8mn over the same period.

In contrast to the sluggish foreign inflows into China equities, domestic investors continued to provide strong liquidity support to the A-share market, particularly through retail participation. New account openings rose 3.6% MoM to 2.86mn in June, bringing the 1H26 total to 20.16mn, up 60.0% YoY. Mutual fund issuance remained robust, with new equity fund launches hitting a fresh YTD high in June. Meanwhile, corporate share buybacks stayed supportive at RMB16.3bn, broadly in line with the RMB17.1bn recorded in May. The key exception has been China's “national team”, which continued to reduce its holdings of broad-market domestic ETFs in June. Even so, as cumulative YTD net outflows have already exceeded the total inflows recorded during 2023-25 – partly reflecting the share price appreciation over the past two years – we expect the pace of such selling to moderate in 2H26.

Hong Kong saw a modest improvement in capital flows, but liquidity conditions remained challenging. Corporate buybacks rose from HKD22.0bn in May to HKD30.2bn in June, the highest monthly level since September 2024, while southbound flows also turned positive at HKD27.1bn after modest outflows in May. However, June inflows were still the third-lowest monthly reading since Mar-2024. Meanwhile, the rotation from Hong Kong equities into A-share persisted, as reflected in continued net redemptions from mainland-listed HK equity ETFs. Although the pace of redemptions eased from the record levels in May, they remain a headwind to Hong Kong market liquidity.

On the capital demand side, IPO financing value rebounded from HKD14.4bn in May to ~HKD40bn in June. Meanwhile, post-IPO lock-up expirations will remain an overhang in 3Q26. Following the recent market pullback, the projected value of restricted share due to unlock in July has declined from ~HKD270bn in our late-May update to ~HKD200bn (primarily driven by MiniMax and Zhipu). Even so, the scale of upcoming unlocks could continue to weigh on market liquidity, in our view. Looking ahead, the value of lock-up expiries is projected to rise further to ~HKD280bn in September.

Macro: export-led, uneven growth

China Investment Compass (CIM) swayed between the C1/recovering and the C4/stimulating phases in 2H24-1Q26, as nominal GDP growth fluctuated around 4.0-4.3%, while monetary policy remained loose. In 2H26, we expect nominal GDP growth to soften modestly, with CIM likely remaining in the C4 phase. Policymakers are likely to prioritize quality growth, self-sufficiency, and continued technological upgrading, rather than resorting to large-scale stimulus measures. As a result, we believe China will remain a stock pickers' market, with alpha generation outweighing beta-driven returns.
Credit and nominal GDP growth will further soften in 2H26

Our forecast of the nominal GDP growth trajectory is based on the credit growth multiplier. As discussed in our earlier reports, China's credit/GDP growth multiplier has been a strong driver and leading indicator to the sequential change in nominal GDP growth. Based on the past experience, the credit multiplier needs to be 1.5-2x for the GDP growth to be sequentially stable (ie flattish QoQ). Over 2.5x multiplier is considered “strong stimulus”, while under 1.5x means “over-tightening”.

China's real GDP growth remained stable at \(5.0\%\) YoY in 1Q26, while nominal GDP growth edged up from \(4.0\%\) in 2025 to \(4.1\%\) in 1Q26. Total credit growth declined from \(8.2\%\) in 2025 to \(7.7\%\) in 1Q26, and further to \(7.4\%\) in May. Credit growth/GDP growth multiplier softened from \(>2x\) in 2H25 to \(1.9x\) in 1Q26, still insufficient to drive a meaningful GDP growth recovery. We continue to expect credit and GDP growth to both edge down modestly in 2026.

Limited prospect of rate cuts

1-year and 5-year Loan Prime Rate (LPR) have been stable since May 2025. Interbank liquidity has been abundant. 3mth SHIBOR declined from 1.9% in Oct-2024 to 1.6% in Dec-25 and further to 1.4% in Jun-2026. Bond yields rebounded in 2H25, partly due to the fund flow out of bonds into equities and the levy of value-added-tax. 10yr CGB yield dropped from 2.2% in Sep-24 to 1.6% in Apr-25, and recovered to 1.9% in Dec-25, before edging down to 1.7% in Jun-2026. Yield on 3yr AAA-rated credit bond declined modestly from 2.1% in Nov-24 to 1.9% in end 2025, and further to 1.7% in Jun-26.

Over the past five years, 1yr/5yr LPR has been cut by 85bp/115bp, while major banks' 1yr/3yr time deposit pricing has been reduced by 80/150bp cumulatively. However, the effectiveness of monetary easing, in terms of boosting consumption, stabilizing property markets, and driving credit demand, has been limited. Given China bank sector's already thin margins and the need to safeguard financial stability, regulators appear reluctant to further cut LPRs this year.

RMB: modest appreciation should be positive to RMB asset prices

RMB to USD exchange rate touched 7.2 in Apr/May 2025, amid the trade wars, but eased back to 7.1 by Dec-25 and 6.8 by Jun-26. Market consensus expects a modest RMB appreciation in 2026. China's FX reserve has also rebounded from USD3.0tn in Sep-2022 to USD3.4tn in May-2026, the highest level since 2016. RMB appreciation should be positive for RMB-dominated asset prices - for instance, China banks' dividend yield could become more attractive in USD terms.

Energy prices, inflation and industrial profits

China's PPI exited a 41-month deflationary period in Mar-26, and accelerated to \(+3.9\%\) by May, consistent with its historical correlation with oil prices. Industrial profit growth improved in tandem, moving from \(-3.3\%\) in 2024 to \(+0.6\%\) YoY in 2025, and accelerating further to \(+18.8\%\) YoY in 5M26 - in line with our prior expectations.
However, sustainability of this reflationary trend and associated profit recovery is questionable. With oil prices retreating to around USD70 by now, the recent momentum is losing support.

Appendix
China Investment Compass (中国投资罗盘)

We believe that China equity markets' performance is driven by the macroeconomic cycle and the monetary policy cycle. Our China Investment Compass defines the past 19 years, since 1Q2007, into four different phases:
• C1: recovering phase, with accelerating GDP growth and loose interbank liquidity;
• C2: peaking phase, with accelerating growth and tight liquidity;
• C3: over-tightening phase, with decelerating growth and tight liquidity; and
• C4: stimulating phase, with decelerating growth and loose liquidity.

China's equity market typically has low beta with flattish return in the C1/recovering phase, while the commodity market is usually strong. The C2/peaking phase is typically a bull market, and the C3/over-tightening phase tends to be a bear market. The C4/stimulating phase is the more volatile times.
Methodology and input factors

Growth is defined as the sequential change in YoY nominal GDP growth (past four quarters cumulative). For instance, if nominal GDP grew by 10% YoY in the last quarter, and 9.5% in the current quarter, the sequential change is -0.5ppt, and it is considered as “growth decelerating”.

Liquidity is calculated based on the quarterly average interbank deposit spread, using 3-month SHIBOR minus 3-month time deposit rate. Deposit spread above 2% is considered “tight liquidity”, and below 2% is considered “loose”.

Stock market performance is partly guided by GDP growth and liquidity cycles, with GDP growth driving earnings and liquidity driving P/E multiples.

China's equity market tends to do well when GDP growth accelerates sequentially and suffers when economy decelerates. In fact, stock market performance tends to lead the GDP performance by 6-12 months. As corporate earnings cycle usually moves in sync with GDP cycle, higher GDP growth and higher earnings can drive market price higher, even without multiple expansion.

Liquidity and monetary policy also impact stock market performance. Monetary tightening can help contain debt leverage and asset price bubbles, and is positive for the long-term health of China's financial system. In the past, China's stock market enjoyed some of the best performance during the C2/peaking phase, with the combination of policy tightening and accelerating growth, eg. 2007 and 2017. On the other side, when GDP growth decelerates, liquidity easing can also help drive strong market performance (eg. in 2H11, 2020). Rich liquidity reduces the cost of capital, and can drive up P/E multiples, so that market can do well in easing phases, without earnings growth.
